nodes.question: What is the range of home range estimates for male individuals?
nodes.answer: Home range estimates for males range from 7.6 to 269.0 hectares.
nodes.paragraph: 2014). The species is regarded as a gregarious, woodland-dwelling mam- mal, and while they occur in a variety of habitats, they are reliant on forests for shelter, with adjacent grasslands to forage (Hill 1981). Home range esti- mates vary widely across land use types, ranging from 7.6 to 269.0 ha for males and 9.3 248.0 ha for females (Neaves et al. 2017; Brunton et al. 2018a, b). Individuals exhibit fission fusion social structures and live in small communities (colloquially termed, mobs), whose habitat use are driven by their access to high-quality foraging habitats (Moss and Rollings 1998; Ramp and Coulson 2004), mating opportuni- ties (Zenger et al. 2003; Coghlan et al. 2016), and predation avoidance (Banks 2001). As a result of these social structures, populations can provide innate ecological support for an ecosystem, such as through native seed germination and dispersal (Claridge et al. 2016). nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What distinguishes the various techniques for analyzing acoustic data?
nodes.answer: The techniques are primarily distinguished by whether the analysis aims to identify species present or summarize the area's acoustic environment (soundscape).
nodes.paragraph: Background & Summary Human activities are accelerating biodiversity loss1. National and international efforts are being made to address this global challenge. In December 2022, countries worldwide committed to the ambitious targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), aiming at halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030 2. A crucial component of the framework is the proper monitoring of progress, including the monitoring of biodiversity patterns3. To achieve this, it is essential to develop effective monitoring technologies capable of assessing biodiversity across large spatial and temporal scales3. When considering vocalizing animals, such as birds, passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) methods have been proposed as a promising approach4. PAM methods involve collecting acoustic data using autonomous recording units, which can then be analyzed to extract ecologically meaningful information about the biodiversity in a spe - cific area of interest5. Multiple techniques for analyzing acoustic data exist, primarily distinguished by whether the analysis aims to identify the species present or summarize the area S acoustic environment (soundscape)6. Species identification techniques usually involve the supervised training of a machine learning algorithm to recognize the acoustic patterns of specific species using a set of annotated acoustic samples.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What time period were the bird surveys conducted for the CBMS monitoring program in 2023?
nodes.answer: The bird surveys were conducted annually between March and June, specifically from March 1st to May 26th, 2023.
nodes.paragraph: For the purposes of the CBMS monitoring program, bird surveys are conducted annually between March and June at ~100 study sites. We collected acoustic data at sixty-one of those sites (Fig. 1) in low-intensity agricultural areas and forest and seminatural areas (Fig. 2) between March 1 st and May 26th, 2023. To identify the land cover at each site, we used ArcGIS Pro (version 2.9) to overlay the GPS locations of each site with the most recent Corine Land Cover map (2018) available at https://land.copernicus.eu/en/products/corine-land-cover . We then used fifteen Song Meter Mini acoustic recorders (Wildlife Acoustics) purchased for the purposes of BIOMON to record audio files at the sixty-one sites. The fifteen recorders were deployed sequentially across the sites. At each site, a recorder was installed on a tree at a height of ~1.5 meters for approximately one week (mean = 7.2 days, min = 7 days, max = 9 days). The device was programmed using the Song Meter mobile app to record 30 audio files per hour, each one minute long 24, for 24 hours per day, resulting in an average of 5,134 audio files per site (min = 4,344 files, max = 6,684 files, standard deviation = 399 files).

nodes.question: What is the purpose of the Dormouse Monitoring System (DoMoS)?
nodes.answer: The purpose of the Dormouse Monitoring System (DoMoS) is to know the site of occurrence of a species and record it together with habitat data.
nodes.paragraph: for wildcats (Stefano et al. 2012). A combination of a weighing module, hair trap and a camera in a plastic tube is used as Dormouse Monitoring System (DoMoS, B chner et al. 2022). These methods have the advantage that the site of occurrence of a species is known, and can be recorded together with habitat data. The non-invasive collection of hair samples (see hair tubes mentioned above, or e.g. lure sticks for wild cats or pine martens (Burki et al. 2010; Steyer et al. 2013) or feces particularly of larger mammal species are commonly com- bined with subsequent determination by molecular tech- niques (Walker et al. 2016). Only rarely and in certain envi- ronments feces of terrestrial small mammals are collected directly in the field, Microtus cabrerae in Portugal (Ferreira et al. 2018). In another case, feces were collected non-inva- sively by using Mouse Bait Stations (Aylward et al. 2022). Recent advances in molecular techniques led to eDNA applications to detect species in an environment that were not directly observed.
